# Oral rehydration (water, salt and sugar) (`oral_rehydration`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by boiled_water, cholera_waterborne
- Core idea: Diarrhoea can cause fatal loss of water and salts within hours. The gut can still absorb sodium together with glucose, and water follows. Mix a standard oral rehydration salts packet with the exact volume of safe water specified. If no packet is available, the emergency household mixture is six level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt in one litre of safe water. Offer frequent small sips, replace ongoing stool losses and continue feeding and breastfeeding. Shock, severe dehydration or inability to drink requires urgent medical care and intravenous fluids.
- Pitfalls:
  - Too much salt, which can kill a child; use level measures and remake a mixture of uncertain strength
  - Withholding drink and food to 'rest the bowel', the traditional and deadly advice
  - Giving plain water only, or sugary drinks without salt
  - Honey for babies under one year (risk of botulism)
  - Stopping when the patient vomits instead of giving smaller sips more often
- History: india: 1953 – H. N. Chatterjee, Calcutta, treats cholera with an oral glucose and salt solution; 1971 Dilip Mahalanabis uses it in refugee camps of the Bangladesh war and reports a case fatality of about 4 % among the patients treated; europe: 1832 – Latta in Scotland revives cholera patients with salt water into a vein, forgotten again; global: 1960 – Crane describes the coupled uptake of sodium and glucose; 1968 trials in Dhaka (Nalin, Cash) and Calcutta (Pierce) show the drink can replace infusions; 1978 adopted by WHO
- Read:
  - David R. Nalin, Richard A. Cash et al., Oral maintenance therapy for cholera in adults, The Lancet (1968)
  - Joshua Nalibow Ruxin, Magic bullet: the history of oral rehydration therapy, Medical History (1994)
  - World Health Organization, Oral Rehydration Salts: Production of the New ORS (2006)
